summary: S01 official NASA NTRS PDF opened HTTP 200; Hermes abstract quote is a splice of real sentences, and 'at or below 8×10−6 Torr' / 'all vacuum tests were performed' are not the page wording (the abstract says 'at less than 8 × 10−6 Torr'). S02 Springer HTML was a bot-check page in this environment, so the journal full text was not opened here. The official TU Dresden-hosted Space Propulsion 2020+1 conference PDF (SP2020_268, same title) was opened HTTP 200; use that wording. Hermes journal-style 'at least two orders of magnitude' is 'more than three orders of magnitude' in the conference abstract; '2 mm-thick' is '2 mm thick'. S03 live NTRS citation URL did not complete here; the official abstract was opened from the Internet Archive snapshot 20261102025427 of that same NTRS URL. A public NTRS PDF link is listed on that page but was not successfully fetched here, so S03 stays abstract only.

rows.note: Official NASA PDF, title 'Measurement of Impulsive Thrust from a Closed Radio Frequency Cavity in Vacuum', authors including Harold White et al., NASA Johnson Space Center / Eagleworks. Abstract wording (line breaks joined): 'A vacuum test campaign evaluating the impulsive thrust performance of a tapered RF test article excited in the TM212 mode at 1,937 megahertz (MHz) has been completed. The test campaign consisted of a forward thrust phase and reverse thrust phase at less than 8 × 10−6 Torr vacuum with power scans at 40 watts, 60 watts, and 80 watts. The test campaign included a null thrust test effort to identify any mundane sources of impulsive thrust, however none were identified. Thrust data from forward, reverse, and null suggests that the system is consistently performing with a thrust to power ratio of 1.2 ± 0.1 mN/kW.' Geometry: 'The RF resonance test article is a copper frustum with an inner diameter of 27.9 cm on the big end, inner diameter of 15.9 cm on the small end, and an axial length of 22.9 cm.' 'The test article contains a 5.4 cm-thick disc of polyethylene with an outer diameter of 15.6 cm that is mounted to the inside face of the smaller diameter end of the frustum.' 'A 13.5 millimeter diameter loop antenna drives the system in the TM212 mode at 1,937 MHz.' Later: 'The results from the null thrust testing show no impulsive element in the collected data, only the thermal signal.' Also: 'a null thrust test effort of three tests performed at vacuum at 80 W'.

Live Springer article URL returned a bot-check page, not the CEAS journal full text. Official TU Dresden Space Propulsion 2020+1 conference PDF SP2020_268, same title, authors M. Tajmar, O. Neunzig, M. Weikert, Institute of Aerospace Engineering, Technische Universität Dresden, was opened HTTP 200. Conference abstract: 'Using a geometry and operating conditions close to the model by White et al that reported positive results published in the peer-reviewed literature, we found no thrust values within a wide frequency band including several resonance frequencies. Our data limits any anomalous thrust to below the force equivalent from classical radiation for a given amount of power. This provides strong limits to all proposed theories and rules out previous test results by more than three orders of magnitude.' Geometry: 'Our cavity is based on the same geometry as the one used by White et al [3] to compare with peer-reviewed results. It consists of a tapered cone, which was mechanically pressed, with a cylindrical flange and a collar made out of 2 mm thick copper as shown in Fig. 7.' 'resonant frequency of 1,914 MHz' and 'unloaded Qu factor of approximately 23,000'. Do not use the Hermes journal wording 'at least two orders of magnitude' or '2 mm-thick copper'. Author emails printed on the PDF were not copied into the research note.

Live NTRS citation URL did not complete in this environment. Official abstract opened from the Internet Archive snapshot of that same NTRS page (2026-11-02). Title on the page: 'Anomalous Thrust Production from an RF Test Device Measured on a Low-Thrust Torsion Pendulum'. Abstract: 'Approximately 30-50 micro-Newtons of thrust were recorded from an electric propulsion test article consisting primarily of a radio frequency (RF) resonant cavity excited at approximately 935 megahertz. Testing was performed on a low-thrust torsion pendulum that is capable of detecting force at a single-digit micronewton level, within a stainless steel vacuum chamber with the door closed but at ambient atmospheric pressure.' 'Thrust was observed on both test articles, even though one of the test articles was designed with the expectation that it would not produce thrust. Specifically, one test article contained internal physical modifications that were designed to produce thrust, while the other did not (with the latter being referred to as the "null" test article).' 'The torsion pendulum was designed, built, and operated by Eagleworks Laboratories at the NASA Johnson Space Center of Houston, Texas.' The snapshot lists a public PDF at /api/citations/20140006052/downloads/20140006052.pdf; that PDF was not successfully fetched here, so this source remains abstract only.
